newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banker frowns on moves to limit bank power.
newsitem.headline: German banker frowns on moves to limit bank power.

text.p: Martin Kohlhaussen, the head of the federation of German banks and Germany's third largest commercial bank Commerzbank, on Sunday criticised efforts to limit German banks' influence and power.

"Considering the dramatic problems we face at the moment, it is almost criminal to see the amount of energy that politicians devote to the topic of the German banks' power," Kohlhaussen told the newspaper Welt am Sonntag.

Noting that Germany's three largest commercial banks, Deutsche Bank, Dresdner Bank and Commerzbank, controlled only 13 percent of the market, Kohlhaussen asked why there was no public debate about the German chemical industry's or the unions' power.
"We all have power, the large banks included. But for me this means: wielding influence also includes taking responsibility for decisions," Kohlhaussen said.
Germany's banks are known to have particularly close relationships with businesses as many of bankers sit on the supervisory boards of Germany's largest companies.
But recently the have come under fire for wielding too much influence and having lost much impartiality.

While Kohlhaussen admitted there were some areas of potential conflict of interest, he vehemently opposed calls for new regulations to sort this out, charging that there were already far too many regulations.
Kohlhaussen was also concerned about plans to chance rules governing proxy voting power as this would hurt the rights of banks' clients.

"If a bank were no longer able to exercise its proxy voting power for its customers as soon as it held more than a five percent stake in a corporation, then this limits the rights of the customer," Kohlhaussen said. "We would have to tell our customers, take your securities account elsewhere."
In recent years the banks have also grabbed headlines as tax authorities swooped down on almost every major institution, searching for evidence that banks had helped Germans avoid tax payments.
Asked whether the steady stream of tax raids has hurt Germany's image as a financial centre, Kohlhaussen said "I hope the worst part is over now, but the tax authorities have cost us a lot of money."
But Kohlhaussen said that banks could not be blamed for private German citizens' decisions. "We don't sign their tax forms," he said.
